text: Welcome to the Isogeny-based Cryptography Wiki. This site serves as an open-source, mathematically rigorous, and accessible repository of knowledge detailing post-quantum cryptographic schemes built on the hardness of finding isogenies between elliptic curves.

title: CSURF
text:
The CSURF scheme is a variant of the CSIDH scheme, designed to operate on the “surface” of the supersingular isogeny graph rather than the “floor” [CaDe20]. CSURF utilizes supersingular elliptic curves over a finite prime field \(\mathbb{F}_p\) (where \(p \equiv 3 \pmod 4\)) whose endomorphism rings are isomorphic to the maximal order \(\mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt{-p})/2]\). This is in contrast to original CSIDH, which relies on curves with the non-maximal endomorphism ring \(\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-p}]\) (the floor).
A key operational advantage of CSURF is unlocked when the prime satisfies \(p \equiv 7 \pmod 8\). In this setting, horizontal 2-isogenies can be efficiently computed to evaluate the class group action. This efficiency stems from the fact that computing these 2-isogenies requires little more than a single exponentiation in the base field \(\mathbb{F}_p\). Additionally, moving to the surface eliminates the redundant \(\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}\) factor present in the acting ideal-class group of standard CSIDH, which provides no extra security.

title: CSURF
text:
2 Scheme Design

2.1 Curve Representation
CSURF relies on a tweaked Montgomery curve representation. The set of valid public keys is defined by the set \[S_p^- = \{A \in \mathbb{F}_p \mid y^2 = x^3 + Ax^2 - x \text{ is supersingular}\}\] This adjusted equation, \(y^2 = x^3 + Ax^2 - x\), allows any curve on the surface to be uniquely represented by its coefficient \(A\). Crucially, the set \(S_p^-\) contains \(0\), making the curve \(y^2 = x^3 - x\) an ideal, natural starting curve \(s_0\) for the scheme.


2.2 Key Exchange
The CSURF scheme models a hard homogeneous space, where a finite commutative group acts freely and transitively on a set. The acting group is the ideal-class group \(\mathcal{C}l(\mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt{-p})/2])\) acting on the set \(S_p^-\) of tweaked Montgomery coefficients.
The steps for a non-interactive key exchange between two parties, Alice and Bob, proceed as follows:

Public Parameters: The system establishes a large prime \(p \equiv 7 \pmod 8\) constructed as \(p = 4 \cdot \prod_{i=1}^n \ell_i - 1\), where \(\ell_i\) are small distinct odd primes, alongside the starting prime \(\ell_0 = 2\). The base curve coefficient is \(E_0 = 0 \in S_p^-\).
Private Key Generation: Alice secretely samples a vector of exponents \((e_0, e_1, \dots, e_n)\) from a designated range. This vector represents an ideal class \([\mathfrak{a}] = [\mathfrak{l}_0^{e_0}\mathfrak{l}_1^{e_1} \dots \mathfrak{l}_n^{e_n}]\) in the class group \(\mathcal{C}l(\mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt{-p})/2])\). For \(\ell_0=2\), the exponent \(e_0\) can be sampled from a much larger interval because 2-isogenies are very fast to compute. Bob similarly samples his own secret exponent vector to form ideal \([\mathfrak{b}]\).
Public Key Evaluation: Alice computes her public key by evaluating the class group action on the starting curve: \(E_A = [\mathfrak{a}] E_0\).

Action Evaluation: To evaluate \([\mathfrak{a}] E_0\), Alice computes a chain of isogenies. Because 2-isogenies are extremely efficient, they are evaluated first without needing to push through points.
For the odd primes \(\ell_i\), Alice generates points of order \(\ell_i\) and uses tweaked Montgomery ladder arithmetic and Vélu’s formulas (requiring just a few sign flips from standard formulas) to compute the odd-degree isogenies and move across the surface graph.
Bob performs the same group action evaluation to compute his public key \(E_B = [\mathfrak{b}] E_0\).

Key Exchange: Alice and Bob exchange their public keys \(E_A\) and \(E_B\) over a public channel.
Shared Secret: Alice computes the shared secret by applying her private group action to Bob’s public key: \(S = [\mathfrak{a}] E_B\). Bob does the corresponding calculation: \(S = [\mathfrak{b}] E_A\). By the commutativity of the class group action, both arrive at the exact same curve coefficient \(S \in S_p^-\), which serves as their shared secret.

title: CSURF
text:
3 Security Assumptions

Hard Homogeneous Spaces: The security of CSURF is rooted in the framework of Hard Homogeneous Spaces originally proposed by Couveignes and Rostovtsev-Stolbunov. The fundamental security assumption is the hardness of the parallelization problem: given a starting element \(s_0\) and elements \(s_1, s_2 \in S\), it must be computationally infeasible to find \(g_1 g_2 * s_0\) where \(s_1 = g_1 * s_0\) and \(s_2 = g_2 * s_0\).
Quantum Resistance: Because the action relies on isogenies of elliptic curves rather than standard cyclic group exponentiation, it does not succumb to Shor’s polynomial-time quantum algorithm. The most efficient known quantum attack against the hard homogeneous space constructed by CSURF is Kuperberg’s algorithm for finding hidden shifts, which operates in subexponential time.
The \(\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}\) Factor and Equivalent Security: A specific topological quirk of the isogeny graph when \(p \equiv 3 \pmod 8\) (the standard CSIDH setting) is the presence of a \(\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}\) factor in the ideal class group \(\mathcal{C}l(\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-p}])\). Operating on the surface inherently avoids this redundant factor, matching the security profile of standard CSIDH.

title: MD-SIDH
text: The Masked-Degree Supersingular Isogeny Diffie-Hellman (MD-SIDH) scheme is a generalization of M-SIDH designed to secure the SIDH key exchange against devastating torsion point attacks. In the original SIDH scheme, the fixed degrees of the secret isogenies, combined with exact torsion point images, allow attackers to embed the secret isogeny into a higher-dimensional isogeny problem and break the scheme. MD-SIDH mitigates this by masking the degree of the secret isogeny [FoMoPe23]. Specifically, the degrees of the secret isogenies are no longer fixed public parameters, but are instead chosen as uniformly random divisors of public smooth integers. To prevent the efficient recovery of this secret degree using Weil pairing computations and discrete logarithms, the scheme requires masking the images of the torsion points by scaling them with a random invertible integer. This ensures the true degree remains hidden, preserving the security of the scheme while facilitating a successful key exchange.

title: MD-SIDH
text:
2 Scheme Design
The MD-SIDH scheme relies on algebraic structures similar to SIDH, but introduces variable secret degrees and masking scalars to obscure the exact torsion point mappings and isogeny degrees.

2.1 Public Parameters
The global parameters dictate the structure of the underlying finite fields and curves.

Security Parameter: Let \(\lambda\) be the target security parameter and let \(t = t(\lambda) \in \mathbb{N}\) be an integer dependent on \(\lambda\).
Isogeny Degree Bounds: Let \(A = l_1^{a_1}\cdots l_t^{a_t}\) and \(B = q_1^{b_1}\cdots q_t^{b_t}\) be two smooth, coprime integers.
Characteristic: Let \(p = ABf - 1\) be a prime, where \(f\) is a small cofactor.
Starting Curve: Let \(E_0\) be a supersingular elliptic curve.
Torsion Bases: The bases for the \(A\)-torsion and \(B\)-torsion subgroups are fixed publicly as \(E_0[A] = \langle P_A, Q_A \rangle\) and \(E_0[B] = \langle P_B, Q_B \rangle\).



2.2 Key Generation and Exchange
During this phase, Alice and Bob generate their secret isogenies using random divisors of the bounds, mask the resulting torsion points with random invertible scalars, and transmit them.
Alice’s Operations:

Secret Key: Alice samples a uniformly random divisor \(A'\) of \(A\) and a random point \(R_A \in E_0[A']\). Her secret key is \(sk_A = R_A\).
Isogeny Computation: She computes the isogeny \(\phi_A: E_0 \rightarrow E_A := E_0/\langle R_A \rangle\) together with the mapped points \(\phi_A(P_B)\) and \(\phi_A(Q_B)\).
Masking Scalar: Alice samples a uniformly random integer \(\alpha \in \mathbb{Z}/B\mathbb{Z}^\times\). The integer \(\alpha\) can be deleted immediately after the public key is generated.
Public Key: Alice masks her output torsion points and publishes her public key as \(pk_A = (E_A, [\alpha]\phi_A(P_B), [\alpha]\phi_A(Q_B))\).

Bob’s Operations:

Secret Key: Bob samples a uniformly random divisor \(B'\) of \(B\) and a random point \(R_B \in E_0[B']\). His secret key is \(sk_B = R_B\).
Isogeny Computation: He computes the isogeny \(\phi_B: E_0 \rightarrow E_B := E_0/\langle R_B \rangle\) together with the mapped points \(\phi_B(P_A)\) and \(\phi_B(Q_A)\).
Masking Scalar: Bob samples a uniformly random integer \(\beta \in \mathbb{Z}/A\mathbb{Z}^\times\). The integer \(\beta\) can be deleted immediately after use.
Public Key: Bob masks his output torsion points and publishes his public key as \(pk_B = (E_B, [\beta]\phi_B(P_A), [\beta]\phi_B(Q_A))\).



2.3 Shared Key Computation
Upon receiving each other’s public keys, the parties use the masked points to recover the unmasked kernels for their respective second-step isogenies.
Alice’s Computation:

Kernel Recovery: From the masked points \([\beta]\phi_B(P_A)\) and \([\beta]\phi_B(Q_A)\), Alice recovers the subgroup \(\langle R'_A \rangle = \langle \phi_B(R_A) \rangle\).
Isogeny Definition: She computes the second-step isogeny defined as \(\phi'_A: E_B \rightarrow E_{AB} := E_B/\langle R'_A \rangle\).
Shared Key: The value \(j(E_{AB})\) is computed as the shared key.

Bob’s Computation:

Kernel Recovery: From the masked points \([\alpha]\phi_A(P_B)\) and \([\alpha]\phi_A(Q_B)\), Bob recovers the subgroup \(\langle R'_B \rangle = \langle \phi_A(R_B) \rangle\).
Isogeny Definition: He computes the second-step isogeny defined as \(\phi'_B: E_A \rightarrow E_{BA} := E_A/\langle R'_B \rangle\).
Shared Key: The value \(j(E_{BA})\) is computed as the shared key.

Due to the commutative nature of the isogeny kernels, \(j(E_{AB}) = j(E_{BA})\), ensuring both parties derive the exact same value as their shared secret.

title: MD-SIDH
text:
3 Security Assumptions
MD-SIDH relies on a modified version of the isogeny with torsion problem, defined as follows:

Let \(E_0/\mathbb{F}_{p^2}\) be a supersingular elliptic curve where \(\#E_0(\mathbb{F}_{p^2}) = (ABf)^2\), with \(E_0[B] = \langle P, Q \rangle\). Let \(A'\) be a uniformly random divisor of \(A\), and let \(\alpha \in \mathbb{Z}/B\mathbb{Z}^\times\) be a random scalar. Given a random \(A'\)-degree isogeny \(\phi: E_0 \rightarrow E_A\), finding \(\phi\) from the public tuple \((E_0, P, Q, E_A, [\alpha]\phi(P), [\alpha]\phi(Q))\) must be computationally infeasible.

Beyond the baseline assumptions of M-SIDH, the security of MD-SIDH critically depends on three specific conditions:

Degree Obfuscation: While the square-free part of the random divisor \(A'\) can be recovered using the Weil pairing, extracting the remaining prime power factors must be mathematically hard.
Unrestricted Scalar Masking: Hiding the torsion point images using any arbitrary invertible integer (\(\alpha\)) must not introduce new structural vulnerabilities, even though it fails to preserve the Weil pairing exactly.
Non-Cyclic Hardness: The core M-SIDH problem must still hold for non-cyclic isogenies. This is required because reducing an MD-SIDH instance (by removing the known square-free degree factors) naturally results in a non-cyclic M-SIDH instance.

title: SimS
text: SimS (Simplified SiGamal) is a post-quantum public-key encryption (PKE) scheme based on supersingular isogenies, specifically introduced to simplify the original SiGamal scheme and achieve stronger security guarantees [FoPe21]. While the canonical PKEs derived from schemes like CSIDH and SIDH are only OW-CPA (One-Way under Chosen Plaintext Attack) secure, requiring hash functions or Fujisaki-Okamoto transformations for higher security, SiGamal provided IND-CPA (Indistinguishability under Chosen-Plaintext Attack) security without hash functions but lacked IND-CCA (Indistinguishability under Chosen-Ciphertext Attack) security. SimS modifies SiGamal to thwart a concrete IND-CCA attack by completely decoupling transmitted curves from their torsion points in the ciphertext. Concretely, SimS replaces the exchanged torsion points with a canonically generated point of smooth order \(2^r\) on a hidden shared curve, and masks its \(x\)-coordinate using a curve-dependent randomizing function. This structural simplification positions SimS between SiGamal and CSIDH, yielding smaller public keys, more compact ciphertexts, and enhanced computational efficiency compared to both SiGamal and C-SiGamal, all while providing IND-CCA security.

title: SimS
text:
2 Scheme Design
SimS operates over a supersingular elliptic curve \(E_0 : y^2 = x^3 + x\) defined over \(\mathbb{F}_p\), where \(p = 2^r \ell_1 \cdots \ell_n - 1\) is a prime such that \(\ell_1, \ldots, \ell_n\) are small distinct odd primes. The scheme relies on the free and transitive action of the ideal class group \(\text{cl}(\mathbb{Z}[\pi])\) on the set of supersingular elliptic curves defined over \(\mathbb{F}_p\) with endomorphism ring \(\mathbb{Z}[\pi]\).
E0E1=[a]E0E3=[b]E0E4=[b]E1;P4=[2m+1]PE4E4=[a]E0;m0=DLP(P4;PE4)[a][b][b][a]

2.1 Setup and Public Parameters

Prime: \(p = 2^r \ell_1 \dots \ell_n - 1\).
Base Curve: \(E_0 : y^2 = x^3 + x\) over \(\mathbb{F}_p\).
Message Space: \(\mathcal{M} = \mathbb{Z}_{2^{r-2}}\).
Randomizing Function: A bijective function \(f_E : \mathbb{F}_p \to \mathbb{F}_p\) indexed by the curve \(E\). A concrete example is \(f_E(x)\) such that its binary representation is \(\text{bin}(x) \oplus \text{bin}(A_E)\), where \(A_E\) is the Montgomery coefficient of \(E\).



2.2 Key Generation

Alice chooses a uniformly random integral ideal class \([\mathfrak{a}]\) from \(\text{cl}(\mathbb{Z}[\pi])\).
She computes the curve \(E_1 = [\mathfrak{a}]E_0\) via the class group action.
Public Key: \(E_1\)
Private Key: \([\mathfrak{a}]\)



2.3 Encryption
To encrypt a plaintext \(m \in \mathbb{Z}_{2^{r-2}}\) for Alice, Bob performs the following steps:

Bob embeds the message \(m\) into \(\mathbb{Z}_{2^r}^\times\) by computing \(M = 2m + 1\).
He chooses a uniformly random ideal class \([\mathfrak{b}] \in \text{cl}(\mathbb{Z}[\pi])\).
He computes the curve \(E_3 = [\mathfrak{b}]E_0\).
He applies the action of \([\mathfrak{b}]\) to Alice’s public key to compute the shared curve \(E_4 = [\mathfrak{b}]E_1 = [\mathfrak{b}][\mathfrak{a}]E_0\).
He uses a deterministic algorithm to canonically generate a point \(P_{E_4} \in E_4(\mathbb{F}_p)\) of smooth order \(2^r\) (where \(2^r \mid p+1\)).
He computes the scalar multiplication \(P_4 = [M]P_{E_4}\).
To avoid leaking the \(x\)-coordinate of \(P_4\) (which could reveal information about \(E_4\)), he masks it using the randomizing function: \(c = f_{E_4}(x(P_4))\).
Ciphertext: \((E_3, c)\)



2.4 Decryption
Upon receiving the ciphertext \((E_3, c)\), Alice performs the following steps:

She computes the shared curve \(E_4 = [\mathfrak{a}]E_3 = [\mathfrak{a}][\mathfrak{b}]E_0\) using her private key \([\mathfrak{a}]\).
Using \(E_4\), she reverses the randomization function to recover \(x(P_4) = f_{E_4}^{-1}(c)\), which identifies the point \(P_4\).
She canonically computes the same base point \(P_{E_4} \in E_4(\mathbb{F}_p)\) of order \(2^r\).
She solves a discrete logarithm problem (DLP) to find the relationship between \(P_4\) and \(P_{E_4}\). Since the group order is \(2^r\) (which is smooth), she can efficiently use the Pohlig-Hellman algorithm to find \(M' \in \mathbb{Z}_{2^r}^\times\) such that \(P_4 = [M']P_{E_4}\).
If \(M' > 2^{r-1}\), she adjusts \(M = 2^r - M'\); otherwise \(M = M'\).
She recovers the original message as \(m = (M - 1) / 2\).

title: SimS
text:
3 Security Assumptions
The security of the SimS scheme rests on two core assumptions:

Commutative Supersingular Isogeny Decisional Diffie-Hellman (CSSIDDH) Assumption: IND-CPA security relies on this assumption. It posits that given a base curve \(E_0\) and two public curves \(E_A = [\mathfrak{a}]E_0\) and \(E_B = [\mathfrak{b}]E_0\), it is computationally infeasible to distinguish the shared secret curve \([\mathfrak{a}][\mathfrak{b}]E_0\) from a uniformly random curve \([\mathfrak{c}]E_0\).
Knowledge of Exponent (KoE)-Type Assumption: IND-CCA security relies on this assumption. It formalizes that if an adversary produces a valid ciphertext \((E_3, c)\), they must be able to extract the underlying ideal class \([\mathfrak{b}]\) used to generate the curve \(E_3 = [\mathfrak{b}]E_0\) and the corresponding masked point on the shared curve \(E_4\).

title: B-SIDH
text:
Broken by a polynomial time classical algorithm.

B-SIDH (pronounced “B-side”) is a novel instantiation that significantly improves upon the original SIDH scheme. It bypasses previous restrictions on the shape of the underlying prime field by permitting parties to operate simultaneously within the \((p+1)\)-torsion of a supersingular elliptic curve and the \((p-1)\)-torsion of its quadratic twist [Cost20].

title: B-SIDH
text:
2 Scheme Design
The B-SIDH scheme structurally mimics the traditional SIDH walk-through but instantiates the operations such that Alice and Bob work in opposite quadratic twists using degrees \(M\) and \(N\), respectively, where \(M |(p+1)\) and \(N | (p-1)\).

2.1 Public Parameters
Unlike traditional SIDH, which requires primes of the restrictive form \(p = f \cdot 2^a 3^b - 1\) (forcing both parties’ smooth degrees to divide \(p+1\)), B-SIDH selects a prime \(p\) such that both \(p+1\) and \(p-1\) are engineered to be smooth, allowing for significantly smaller primes.
The scheme specifies a starting supersingular curve \(E_0 / \mathbb{F}_{p^2}\). It also establishes a basis \(\{P_A, Q_A\}\) for the \(M\)-torsion in \(E_0(\mathbb{F}_{p^2})\) and a basis \(\{P_B, Q_B\}\) for the \(N\)-torsion corresponding to the quadratic twist. Because Montgomery arithmetic is twist-agnostic, coordinates from both sets are processed identically using their \(x\)-coordinates over \(\mathbb{F}_{p^2}\).


2.2 Alice’s Key Generation

Alice chooses two secret integers \((\alpha_A, \beta_A) \in \mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z}\).
She computes her secret point \(S_A = [\alpha_A]P_A + [\beta_A]Q_A\) of order \(M\) from the \((p+1)\)-torsion.
She uses \(S_A\) to compute her secret \(M\)-isogeny \(\phi_A : E_0 \rightarrow E_A\), where \(E_A = E_0 / \langle S_A \rangle\). Because \(p+1\) is engineered to be smooth but may contain larger prime factors than traditional SIDH, computing her secret isogeny requires composing walks of multiple prime degrees (\(l\)-isogenies). Evaluating these larger \(l\)-isogenies in practice is accelerated using \(\sqrt{élu}\).
During the isogeny computation, she maps Bob’s basis points \(P_B\) and \(Q_B\) through \(\phi_A\).
Alice’s Public Key: \(PK_A = (E_A, \phi_A(P_B), \phi_A(Q_B))\).



2.3 Bob’s Key Generation

Bob chooses two secret integers \((\alpha_B, \beta_B) \in \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}\).
He computes his secret point \(S_B = [\alpha_B]P_B + [\beta_B]Q_B\) of order \(N\) from the \((p-1)\)-torsion (on the quadratic twist).
He uses \(S_B\) to compute his secret \(N\)-isogeny \(\phi_B : E_0 \rightarrow E_B\), where \(E_B = E_0 / \langle S_B \rangle\). Just like Alice, Bob’s \(N\)-isogeny computation involves larger prime factors from \(p-1\) and applies the same \(\sqrt{élu}\).
During his isogeny computation, he maps Alice’s basis points \(P_A\) and \(Q_A\) through \(\phi_B\).
Bob’s Public Key: \(PK_B = (E_B, \phi_B(P_A), \phi_B(Q_A))\).



2.4 Shared Secret Computation

Alice: Upon receiving \(PK_B\), Alice uses her secret integers to compute a new point \(S'_A = [\alpha_A]\phi_B(P_A) + [\beta_A]\phi_B(Q_A)\) of order \(M\) on curve \(E_B\). She computes the \(M\)-isogeny \(\phi'_A: E_B \rightarrow E_B / \langle S'_A \rangle\).
Bob: Upon receiving \(PK_A\), Bob uses his secret integers to compute a new point \(S'_B = [\alpha_B]\phi_A(P_B) + [\beta_B]\phi_A(Q_B)\) of order \(N\) on curve \(E_A\). He computes the \(N\)-isogeny \(\phi'_B: E_A \rightarrow E_A / \langle S'_B \rangle\).
Both parties successfully arrive at the same shared secret by computing the j-invariant of their respective final image curves, as \(E_B / \langle S'_A \rangle \cong E_A / \langle S'_B \rangle\).

title: PIKE
text: PIKE (Pairing-assisted Isogeny-based Key Encryption) is a public key encryption scheme that builds upon the recent ElGamal-type POKÉ design framework [CCLL26]. While POKÉ relies on deriving a shared secret on a higher-dimensional, SIDH-like commutative diagram through basis evaluations and solving discrete logarithms, PIKE modifies this approach by using bilinear pairings to establish the shared secret. This careful integration of pairings preserves post-quantum security while bringing two distinct advantages: it yields faster decryption by bypassing the discrete logarithm step entirely, and it significantly relaxes the required prime form. Consequently, PIKE can operate over smaller prime fields, yielding faster overall runtime performance and competitive compactness compared to other isogeny schemes.

2 Scheme Design
Just like POKÉ, the PIKE scheme relies on establishing a commutative diagram between two parties (Alice and Bob) using separate sets of torsion points.

2.1 Public Parameters
The scheme is built on a finite field where the parameters scale strictly with the targeted security parameter \(\lambda\).

\(p\): A prime chosen such that \(2^a C D\) divides \(p^2-1\).

\(a\):To resist brute-force message-recovery attacks against the masking nonce, \(a\) must be chosen such that \(a \approx \lambda\).
\(C\): A smooth integer chosen such that \(C \ge 2^{2\lambda}\). Its size is dictated by the need to prevent \(O(\sqrt{C})\) meet-in-the-middle attacks against the secret isogeny.
\(D\): An integer dividing \(p^2 - 1\), chosen such that \(D \ge 2^\lambda\). This minimum size guarantees \(\lambda\)-bit resistance against direct brute-force guesses of the shared secret pairing value.

\(E_0\): A starting supersingular elliptic curve defined over \(\mathbb{F}_{p^2}\) with a known endomorphism ring.
\(\{P_0, Q_0\}\): A basis of the \(2^a\)-torsion subgroup \(E_0[2^a]\).
\(\{R_0, S_0\}\): A basis of the \(C\)-torsion subgroup \(E_0[C]\).
\(\{X_0, Y_0\}\): A basis of the \(D\)-torsion subgroup \(E_0[D]\).
\(w_0 = e_D(X_0, Y_0)\): The precomputed Weil pairing value of the \(D\)-torsion basis, defined over \(\mathbb{F}_{p^2}\).
\(\text{H}\): A cryptographic hash function modeled as a random oracle. To derive the plaintext pad, it is evaluated with a specific domain-separator prefix as \(\text{H}(\text{KDF} \parallel \cdot)\).

The public parameters for PIKE are defined as \(\mathsf{pp} = (p, a, C, D, E_0, (P_0, Q_0), (R_0, S_0), (X_0, Y_0), w_0)\).


2.2 Key Generation (Alice)
The receiver (Alice) computes a secret isogeny and masked basis evaluations to form the public key.

Secret Prime Selection: Alice samples a positive integer \(q < 2^a\) such that \(q(2^a - q)\) is coprime to \(2\), \(C\), and \(D\).
Secret Isogeny: She generates a random isogeny \(\phi: E_0 \rightarrow E_A\) of degree \(q(2^a - q)\) by adapting RandIsogImages algorithm proposed in QFESTA.
Masking Scalars: Alice randomly samples \(\alpha_2, \beta_2 \in (\mathbb{Z}/2^a\mathbb{Z})^\times\), \(\gamma_C \in (\mathbb{Z}/C\mathbb{Z})^\times\), and \(\delta_D \in (\mathbb{Z}/D\mathbb{Z})^\times\).
Basis Evaluation: She evaluates \(\phi\) on the torsion bases and masks them using the scalars:

\(P_A = [\alpha_2]\phi(P_0)\), \(Q_A = [\beta_2]\phi(Q_0)\)
\(R_A = [\gamma_C]\phi(R_0)\), \(S_A = [\gamma_C]\phi(S_0)\). And \(\gamma_C\) is deleted.
\(X_A = [\delta_D]\phi(X_0)\)

Output:

Secret Key \(\mathsf{sk} = \{q, \alpha_2, \beta_2, \delta_D\}\).
Public Key \(\mathsf{pk} = \{E_A, P_A, Q_A, R_A, S_A, X_A\}\).




2.3 Encryption (Bob)
The sender (Bob) encrypts a message \(\text{msg} \in \{0,1\}^{2\lambda}\) using the public key.

Nonce Selection: Bob samples \(r_3 \in \mathbb{Z}/C\mathbb{Z}\) uniformly at random, alongside random masking scalars \(\omega_2 \in (\mathbb{Z}/2^a\mathbb{Z})^\times\), and \(\eta_D, \zeta_D \in (\mathbb{Z}/D\mathbb{Z})^\times\).
Shared Secret Hash: Bob computes the plaintext padding \(\text{pad} = \text{H}(KDF || tr(w_0^{\eta_D \zeta_D}))\), where \(tr\) denotes the trace over \(\mathbb{F}_p\) to avoid ambiguity in coordinate transmission.
Sender Isogenies: Bob computes a 1-dimensional isogeny \(\psi: E_0 \rightarrow E_B\) of degree \(C\) with kernel \(\langle R_0 + [r_3]S_0 \rangle\). Concurrently, he computes the parallel isogeny \(\psi': E_A \rightarrow E_{AB}\) with kernel \(\langle R_A + [r_3]S_A \rangle\).
Masked Evaluations: Bob evaluates these isogenies on the remaining torsion points:

On \(E_B\):

\(P_B = [\omega_2]\psi(P_0)\),
\(Q_B = [1/\omega_2]\psi(Q_0)\),
\(Y_B = [\eta_D]\psi(Y_0)\)

On \(E_{AB}\):

\(P_{AB} = [\omega_2]\psi'(P_A)\),
\(Q_{AB} = [1/\omega_2]\psi'(Q_A)\),
\(X_{AB} = [\zeta_D]\psi'(X_A)\)


Output: The ciphertext \(\mathsf{ct} = (E_B, P_B, Q_B, Y_B, E_{AB}, P_{AB}, Q_{AB}, X_{AB}, \text{pad} \oplus \text{msg})\).



2.4 Decryption (Alice)
Alice’s goal is to reconstruct the exact shared pairing value Bob used, \(w_0^{\eta_D \zeta_D}\), without knowing Bob’s secret scalars (\(\eta_D, \zeta_D\)). She achieves this by mapping Bob’s public points to a “middle” curve and using her own secret key to strip away the mathematical pollution.

Construct the 2D Isogeny: Alice uses her secret key (\(q, \alpha_2, \beta_2\)) alongside the \(2^a\)-torsion points from the ciphertext (\(P_B, Q_B, P_{AB}, Q_{AB}\)) to construct a 2-dimensional isogeny \(\Phi: E_B \times E_{AB} \rightarrow E_M \times E\). Kani’s Lemma guarantees that the kernel of this isogeny is \(\langle ([-q]P_B, [1/\alpha_2]P_{AB}), ([-q]Q_B, [1/\beta_2]Q_{AB}) \rangle\).
Map to the Middle Curve (\(E_M\)): Alice pushes the \(D\)-torsion points provided by Bob (\(Y_B\) and \(X_{AB}\)) through this 2-dimensional isogeny. This maps them to a new, shared “middle” curve, \(E_M\).

\((X_M, \_) = \Phi(O_{E_B}, X_{AB})\)
\((Y_M, \_) = \Phi(Y_B, O_{E_{AB}})\)

Compute the Polluted Pairing: Alice calculates the Weil pairing of these two new points on the middle curve: \(w = e_D(X_M, Y_M)\). Due to the properties of the commutative diagram, this pairing contains Bob’s secret combined with Alice’s parameters: \[w = e_D(X_0, Y_0)^{q(2^a - q) C \cdot \delta_D \cdot \eta_D \zeta_D}\]
Unmasking (Scalar Inversion): To strip away her own variables (\(q, \delta_D\)) and the public constants (\(2^a, C\)) from the exponent, Alice computes their modular inverse: \[t = [ \delta_D \cdot C \cdot q(2^a - q) ]^{-1} \pmod D\] She raises the polluted pairing \(w\) to this power \(t\), perfectly isolating Bob’s shared secret: \[w^t = e_D(X_0, Y_0)^{\eta_D \zeta_D} = w_0^{\eta_D \zeta_D}\]
Message Recovery: Alice takes the \(\mathbb{F}_p\)-trace of this recovered value and hashes it to recreate the padding, denoted as \(\widetilde{\text{pad}}\). She then XORs this recreated padding against the ciphertext component to read the original message: \[\widetilde{\text{pad}} = H(\text{KDF} \parallel tr(w^t))\] \[\text{msg} = \widetilde{\text{pad}} \oplus (\text{pad} \oplus \text{msg})\]

3 Security Assumptions
PIKE’s IND-CPA security reduces to the underlying Computational-PIKE (C-PIKE) problem in the random oracle model.

The C-PIKE Problem: Given the public parameters and the protocol’s transmitted tuple \((E_A, P_A, Q_A, R_A, S_A, X_A)\) and \((P_B, Q_B, Y_B, P_{AB}, Q_{AB}, X_{AB})\), an adversary must compute the target pairing value \(e_D(X_0, Y_0)^{\eta_D \zeta_D}\). The problem bears heuristic equivalence to C-LIT-SiGamal where \(X_A, X_B, X_{AB}\) are revealed. However, there is no known one-sided reduction between C-PIKE and C-POKÉ.
Resistance to Concrete Attacks: The core of the C-PIKE problem assumes the hardness of the Receiver Isogeny Recovery Problem and the Sender Isogeny Recovery Problem. The masking scalars (\(\alpha_2, \beta_2, \gamma_C, \delta_D\)) are drawn randomly and independently, which neutralizes the vulnerabilities exploited by SIDH key-recovery attacks. Furthermore, the scheme resists meet-in-the-middle attacks and variants mapped in FESTA by keeping torsion points evaluated sufficiently masked or restricted.

title: FESTA
text:
2 Scheme Design
The foundation of FESTA is an injective trapdoor function evaluated over supersingular elliptic curves. By scaling the revealed torsion points with a secret matrix, FESTA prevents malicious attackers from utilizing the SIDH attacks. Using standard transformations (like OAEP), this trapdoor mechanism enables the construction of an efficient IND-CCA secure PKE in the Quantum Random Oracle Model (QROM).

2.1 Global Parameters

\(p\): A prime defined as \(2^b d_1 (d_A)_{sf} d_2 f - 1\), where \(d_1, d_2, d_A\) are smooth numbers and \((d_A)_{sf}\) is the square free part of \(d_A\).
\(E_0\): A starting supersingular elliptic curve defined over \(\mathbb{F}_{p^2}\) (chosen with \(j(E_0) \neq 0, 1728\) to avoid non-trivial automorphisms).
\(\langle P_b, Q_b \rangle = E_0[2^b]\): A canonical basis for the \(2^b\)-torsion on \(E_0\).
\(\mathcal{M}_b\): A set of commutative, invertible diagonal matrices over \((\mathbb{Z}/2^b\mathbb{Z})^\times\) modulo \(\langle -I_2 \rangle\).



2.2 Setup and Key Generation
The trapdoor key generation works as follows:

Compute a secret \(d_A\)-isogeny \(\varphi_A: E_0 \rightarrow E_A\).
Sample a random matrix \(\mathbf{A} \in \mathcal{M}_b\).
Calculate the scaled torsion images on \(E_A\): \[ \begin{pmatrix} R_A \\ S_A \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{A} \begin{pmatrix} \varphi_A(P_b) \\ \varphi_A(Q_b) \end{pmatrix} \]


Secret Key (Trapdoor): \((\mathbf{A}, \varphi_A)\).
Public Key: \((E_A, R_A, S_A)\).



2.3 Function Evaluation (Forward Direction)
To evaluate the one-way function on an input consisting of two isogenies \(\varphi_1: E_0 \rightarrow E_1\) (degree \(d_1\)), \(\varphi_2: E_A \rightarrow E_2\) (degree \(d_2\)), and a matrix \(\mathbf{B} \in \mathcal{M}_b\):

Compute \(\varphi_1: E_0 \rightarrow E_1\) and \(\varphi_2: E_A \rightarrow E_2\).
Scale the torsion basis images under \(\varphi_1\) by \(\mathbf{B}\): \[ \begin{pmatrix} R_1 \\ S_1 \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{B} \begin{pmatrix} \varphi_1(P_b) \\ \varphi_1(Q_b) \end{pmatrix} \]
Scale the public torsion parameters under \(\varphi_2\) by \(\mathbf{B}\): \[ \begin{pmatrix} R_2 \\ S_2 \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{B} \begin{pmatrix} \varphi_2(R_A) \\ \varphi_2(S_A) \end{pmatrix} \]


Output: The tuple \((E_1, R_1, S_1, E_2, R_2, S_2)\).

Without the knowledge of \(\mathbf{A}\), the scaling by \(\mathbf{B}\) (and natively \(\mathbf{A}\)) thoroughly obfuscates the torsion point information, blocking the SIDH attack machinery.


2.4 Trapdoor Inversion
The trapdoor owner can invert the function by utilizing the commutativity of matrices \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\):

Undo the secret scaling on \(E_2\) by applying \(d_1 \mathbf{A}^{-1}\): \[ \begin{pmatrix} R_2' \\ S_2' \end{pmatrix} = d_1 \mathbf{A}^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} R_2 \\ S_2 \end{pmatrix} \] Because \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) commute, this effectively isolates the scaling to just \(\mathbf{B}\), bridging the torsion mappings between \(E_1\) and \(E_2\).
The resulting points reflect the exact unscaled images of \(R_1, S_1\) under the bridging isogeny \(\psi := \varphi_2 \circ \varphi_A \circ \hat{\varphi}_1\).
Invoke an arbitrary torsion-point attack (e.g., Kani’s criterion generalizing to higher dimensions via (2,2)-isogenies) on \((E_1, R_1, S_1, E_2, R_2', S_2')\) to efficiently compute \(\psi\).
Reconstruct the original kernels of \(\varphi_1, \varphi_2\) and the matrix \(\mathbf{B}\) from \(\psi\).

FESTA introduces generalized hardness assumptions for the scaled-torsion setting.

Decisional Isogeny with Scaled-Torsion (DIST): Distinguishing a curve and its scaled torsion images (via matrix \(A\)) from a random supersingular curve and random basis points.
Computational Isogeny with Scaled-Torsion (CIST): Extracting the isogeny \(\varphi\) given \(E_0, E_1\), the domain basis, and the scaled target basis \(\mathbf{A}(\varphi(P_0), \varphi(Q_0))^T\).
Computational Isogeny with Double Scaled-Torsion (CIST\(^2\)): Recovering two distinct isogenies \(\varphi, \varphi'\) given two instances of scaled target bases that use the same scaling matrix \(\mathbf{A}\).

title: CSIDH
text: CSIDH is a post-quantum commutative group action based scheme that enables non-interactive key exchange [CLMP18]. The construction adapts the layout of earlier cryptosystems proposed by Couveignes and Rostovtsev-Stolbunov, but replaces the use of ordinary elliptic curves with supersingular elliptic curves defined over a large prime field \(\mathbb{F}_p\). A key advantage of using supersingular curves over \(\mathbb{F}_p\) (for \(p \ge 5\)) is that they always have exactly \(p + 1\) rational points, which trivially yields the highly composite order needed for efficiency.

title: CSIDH
text:
2 Scheme Design
The core of the CSIDH scheme is based on the free and transitive action of the ideal-class group \(cl(\mathcal{O})\) on the set of \(\mathbb{F}_p\)-isomorphism classes of supersingular elliptic curves with an \(\mathbb{F}_p\)-rational endomorphism ring isomorphic to \(\mathcal{O}\).

2.1 Parameters
The scheme fixes a large prime \(p\) of the form \(4 \cdot \ell_1 \cdots \ell_n - 1\), where \(\ell_i\) are small, distinct odd primes. The base curve is defined as \(E_0 : y^2 = x^3 + x\) over \(\mathbb{F}_p\). The requirement that \(p \equiv 3 \pmod 4\) ensures that \(E_0\) is supersingular and permits the use of efficient Montgomery arithmetic.


2.2 Endomorphism Ring & Isogenies
The Frobenius endomorphism \(\pi\) of \(E_0\) satisfies \(\pi^2 = -p\), giving an \(\mathbb{F}_p\)-rational endomorphism ring of \(\mathcal{O} = \mathbb{Z}[\pi]\). Because \(\pi^2 - 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{\ell_i}\), the ideals \(\ell_i\mathcal{O}\) split into Elkies primes \(\mathfrak{l}_i = (\ell_i, \pi - 1)\) and \(\bar{\mathfrak{l}}_i = (\ell_i, \pi + 1)\). The isogenies for \(\mathfrak{l}_i\) can be evaluated efficiently because their kernels are generated by points of order \(\ell_i\) that lie in the kernel of \(\pi - 1\), meaning they are rational over the base field \(\mathbb{F}_p\).


2.3 Private Key
A private key is constructed as an exponent vector \((e_1, \dots, e_n)\) with each \(e_i \in \{-m, \dots, m\}\), representing the ideal class \([\mathfrak{l}_1^{e_1} \mathfrak{l}_2^{e_2} \cdots \mathfrak{l}_n^{e_n}] \in cl(\mathcal{O})\).


2.4 Public Key
An individual’s public key (e.g., Alice’s key \(A\)) is the Montgomery coefficient of the curve \(E_A : y^2 = x^3 + Ax^2 + x\), which is obtained by applying the action of the secret key \([a]\) to the base curve \(E_0\).


2.5 Key Exchange
When Alice receives Bob’s public key \(B\), she first verifies that the curve \(E_B\) is supersingular. She then applies her secret ideal class action \([\mathfrak{a}]\) to compute \([\mathfrak{a}]E_B = [\mathfrak{a}][\mathfrak{b}]E_0\). The shared secret is the unique Montgomery coefficient \(S\) corresponding to the combined curve \([\mathfrak{a}][\mathfrak{b}]E_0\).

title: CSIDH
text:
3 Security Assumptions
The security of the CSIDH scheme relies on the hardness of an isogeny-finding problem analogous to the classical discrete logarithm problem.

Key Recovery Problem: The fundamental computational assumption is that given two supersingular elliptic curves \(E\) and \(E'\) over \(\mathbb{F}_p\) with the same \(\mathbb{F}_p\)-rational endomorphism ring \(\mathcal{O}\), it is computationally infeasible to find an ideal \(\mathfrak{a}\) such that \([\mathfrak{a}]E = E'\).
Quantum Security: Breaking the scheme translates to solving an instance of the abelian hidden-shift problem. This problem can be addressed using subexponential-time quantum algorithms, such as those proposed by Kuperberg. The precise asymptotic complexity depends heavily on the cost of computing the isogeny oracle; combinations of algorithms yield bounds in the realm of \(L_p[1/2, 1/\sqrt{2}]\).
Chosen-Ciphertext Security: Because CSIDH naturally affords efficient public-key validation, it avoids vulnerabilities related to the reuse of dishonest keys. This validation allows CSIDH to securely achieve non-interactive key exchange without resorting to additional chosen-ciphertext attack (CCA) transformations like the Fujisaki-Okamoto transform.

title: binSIDH
text: The binSIDH scheme is designed to provide a secure and efficient isogeny-based key exchange in the wake of the polynomial-time key-recovery attacks that broke the original SIDH scheme [BaFo23]. Originally, SIDH required revealing the images of torsion points to enable parties to compute parallel isogenies and arrive at a shared secret, but this extra torsion information was ultimately exploited to recover the secret isogeny. To circumvent these attacks without sacrificing the efficiency of SIDH too heavily, binSIDH introduces the concept of “artificially oriented curves.” By equipping an elliptic curve with a pair of cyclic disjoint subgroups (an artificial orientation), the scheme limits the set of allowable isogenies and restricts the revealed information strictly to the push-forwards of these orientations. This formulation interpolates between the original SIDH and group-action based schemes (like CSIDH), revealing sufficiently less information to prevent the known torsion-based attacks while preserving the parallel isogeny structure necessary for a Diffie-Hellman-like key agreement.

text:
2 Scheme Design
The binSIDH scheme restricts computations to full-degree artificially oriented isogenies. Below is a detailed walkthrough of the scheme setup, key generation, and shared key derivation.

2.1 Setup
The public parameters are generated as follows:

\(\lambda\): The security parameter (e.g., 128, 192, 256) that dictates the targeted security level.
\(t\): An integer depending on \(\lambda\), representing the number of distinct prime factors required to achieve the desired security.
\(l_i, q_i\): Small, distinct prime numbers for \(i \in \{1, \dots, t\}\).
\(A, B\): Coprime integers where \(A = \prod_{i=1}^t l_i\) and \(B = \prod_{i=1}^t q_i\). \(A\) dictates the degree of Alice’s isogenies, while \(B\) dictates Bob’s. The values are chosen such that \(A \approx B \approx \sqrt{p}\).
\(f\): A small cofactor used to ensure the resulting \(p\) is a valid prime.
\(p\): A large prime of the form \(p = ABf - 1\).
\(E_0\): A starting supersingular elliptic curve defined over \(\mathbb{F}_{p^2}\) with cardinality \(\#E_0(\mathbb{F}_{p^2}) = (p+1)^2\). To avoid special endomorphism ring properties that could lead to attacks, this curve should be generated via a uniformly random walk.
\(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{B}\): Artificial orientations on \(E_0\). Specifically, the artificial \(A\)-orientation is defined as \(\mathfrak{A} = (G_1, G_2)\), where \(G_1, G_2 \subset E_0[A]\) are cyclic disjoint subgroups of order \(A\). The artificial \(B\)-orientation is similarly defined as \(\mathfrak{B} = (H_1, H_2)\), a pair of cyclic disjoint subgroups of order \(B\).

The globally public parameters are \((E_0, p, A, B, \mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{B})\).


2.2 Key Generation
Both parties independently sample random secret vectors that dictate the specific subgroups used to construct their secret isogenies.
Alice:

Samples a secret vector \(\mathbf{a}\) uniformly at random from \(\{1, 2\}^t\).
Decomposes her artificial \(A\)-orientation \(\mathfrak{A} = (G_1, G_2)\). Since \(G_1\) and \(G_2\) are cyclic groups of order \(A = \prod_{i=1}^t l_i\), they can be written as the direct sum of their prime-order components: \(G_1 = G_1^1 \oplus \dots \oplus G_1^t\) and \(G_2 = G_2^1 \oplus \dots \oplus G_2^t\), where each \(G_1^i\) and \(G_2^i\) has order \(l_i\).
Constructs the \(\mathfrak{A}\)-isogeny \(\phi_A : E_0 \to E_A\) of degree \(A\). The kernel of \(\phi_A\) is strictly dictated by the vector \(\mathbf{a}\): for each \(i\)-th prime factor \(l_i\), she selects the kernel component from either \(G_1^i\) (if \(\mathbf{a}_i = 1\)) or \(G_2^i\) (if \(\mathbf{a}_i = 2\)). Formally, \(\ker \phi_A = \langle G_{\mathbf{a}_1}^1, G_{\mathbf{a}_2}^2, \dots, G_{\mathbf{a}_t}^t \rangle\).
Computes the image of Bob’s artificial \(B\)-orientation \(\mathfrak{B}\) under her isogeny. This is simply the evaluation of \(\phi_A\) on the subgroups of \(\mathfrak{B}\), yielding \(\mathfrak{B}' = \phi_A(\mathfrak{B}) = (\phi_A(H_1),\phi_A(H_2))\).
Alice’s secret key is \(\mathbf{a}\) and her public key is \((E_A, \mathfrak{B}')\).

Bob:

Samples a secret vector \(\mathbf{b}\) uniformly at random from \(\{1, 2\}^t\).
Decomposes his artificial \(B\)-orientation \(\mathfrak{B} = (H_1, H_2)\) into its prime-order components \(H_1^i\) and \(H_2^i\) of order \(q_i\).
Constructs the \(\mathfrak{B}\)-isogeny \(\phi_B : E_0 \to E_B\) of degree \(B\). The kernel is chosen from \(\mathfrak{B}\) according to the vector \(\mathbf{b}\), such that \(\ker \phi_B = \langle H_{\mathbf{b}_1}^1, H_{\mathbf{b}_2}^2, \dots, H_{\mathbf{b}_t}^t \rangle\).
Computes the image of Alice’s artificial \(A\)-orientation \(\mathfrak{A}\) under his isogeny, yielding \(\mathfrak{A}' = \phi_B(\mathfrak{A})\).
Bob’s secret key is \(\mathbf{b}\) and his public key is \((E_B, \mathfrak{A}')\).



2.3 Shared Key Computation
Upon exchanging public keys, the parties compute their parallel isogenies to arrive at a common curve.
Alice:

Receives Bob’s public key \((E_B, \mathfrak{A}')\). She verifies that \(\mathfrak{A}'\) is indeed a valid artificial \(A\)-orientation on \(E_B\); if not, she aborts.
She computes the \(\mathfrak{A}'\)-isogeny \(\phi_A' : E_B \to E_{BA}\) of degree \(A\), defined by her secret vector \(\mathbf{a}\).
Her shared key is the \(j\)-invariant of the resulting curve, \(j(E_{BA})\).

Bob:

Receives Alice’s public key \((E_A, \mathfrak{B}')\). He verifies that \(\mathfrak{B}'\) is a valid artificial \(B\)-orientation on \(E_A\); if not, he aborts.
He computes the \(\mathfrak{B}'\)-isogeny \(\phi_B' : E_A \to E_{AB}\) of degree \(B\), defined by his secret vector \(\mathbf{b}\).
His shared key is the \(j\)-invariant of the resulting curve, \(j(E_{AB})\).

Due to the structure of parallel isogenies over artificially oriented curves, the resulting codomain curves \(E_{AB}\) and \(E_{BA}\) are isomorphic, ensuring \(j(E_{AB}) = j(E_{BA})\).

3 Security Assumptions
The security of binSIDH relies on a set of computational problems related to artificially oriented curves, some of which are generalizations of recently introduced isogeny problems.

Supersingular Isogeny Problem for artificially A-oriented curves (SSIP-A): Given an artificially \(A\)-oriented curve \((E, \mathfrak{A})\), a codomain curve \(E'\), the image orientation \(\mathfrak{A}'\), and a degree \(B\), compute the isogeny of degree \(B\) connecting them. This is a generalization of the CIST problem previously introduced in the FESTA cryptosystem.
Artificially Oriented Isogeny Problem (AOIP): Given a starting curve \(E\) with an artificial \(A\)-orientation \(\mathfrak{A}\) and an artificial \(B\)-orientation \(\mathfrak{B}\), along with the codomain curve \(E'\) and the image orientation \(\mathfrak{A}'\), compute the cyclic \(B\)-isogeny.
Artificially Oriented Computational Diffie-Hellman (AO-CDH): Given the initial public parameters and the two public keys \((E_A, \phi_A(\mathfrak{B}))\) and \((E_B, \phi_B(\mathfrak{A}))\), compute the shared invariant \(j(E_{AB})\).

title: QFESTA
text:
QFESTA (Quaternion Fast Encapsulation from Supersingular Torsion Attacks) is a new isogeny-based public-key encryption (PKE) and key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) based on the FESTA scheme [NaOn24]. The main innovation in QFESTA’s design is the sub-algorithm RandIsogImages, which evaluates non-smooth degree isogenies using Kani’s lemma and quaternion endomorphisms. Finally, to achieve indistinguishability against chosen ciphertext attacks (IND-CCA) in the quantum random oracle model (QROM), the core One-Way Chosen Plaintext Attack (OW-CPA) secure PKE is wrapped using the Fujisaki-Okamoto (\(FO^{\not\perp}\)) transform.


Given a special supersingular elliptic curve \(E_0/\mathbb{F}_{p^2}\) with \(j\)-invariant 1728, its known maximal order \(\mathcal{O}_0 \cong \text{End}(E_0)\), and an target non-smooth isogeny degree \(d\):

2 Scheme Design
FESTA uses the SIDH attack machinery for decryption, which natively imposes strong smoothness constraints on the degrees of the underlying isogenies (\(d_A, d_1, d_2\)), forcing them to be large and leading to significant data sizes and computational overhead. To circumvent these limitations, QFESTA introduces a novel technique leveraging quaternion algebras to compute the codomain and point images of non-smooth degree isogenies from a special starting curve. This eliminates the smoothness restriction for degrees \(d_A\) and \(d_1\), vastly shrinking parameter sizes.

2.1 System Setup and Parameters
Before key generation, the system initializes global parameters based on a chosen security parameter \(\lambda\). This setup routine computes the necessary constants and defines the mathematical structures used by all parties:

Degree Exponents (\(a, b\)): To achieve the desired security level, the protocol sets \(b = \lceil \log_3 2^\lambda \rceil\) and \(a = \lceil \log_2 (2^\lambda + 3^b) \rceil\). This ensures the sizes of the isogeny walks are properly balanced.
Secret Isogeny Degrees (\(d_{A,1}, d_1\)): Using the exponents above, the non-smooth isogeny degrees are defined as \(d_{A,1} = 2^a - 3^b\) and \(d_1 = 2^{2a} + 2^a \cdot 3^b + 3^{2b}\).
Characteristic (\(p\)): A prime \(p\) is calculated as \(p = 2^{3a} \cdot 3f - 1\), where \(f\) is a small positive integer found by ascending search until \(p\) is prime.
Base Curve and Ring: The initial supersingular elliptic curve is defined over \(\mathbb{F}_{p^2}\) as \(E_0 : y^2 = x^3 + x\), and its known endomorphism ring is \(\mathcal{O}_0 = \mathbb{Z}\langle1, i, \frac{i+j}{2}, \frac{1+k}{2}\rangle\).
Torsion Basis: A basis \((P_0, Q_0)\) is established for the \(2^{3a}\)-torsion subgroup \(E_0[2^{3a}]\).
Matrix Space (\(\mathcal{M}_{2^{3a}}\)): Let \(\mathcal{M}_{2^{3a}}\) denote the set of \(2 \times 2\) diagonal invertible matrices over the ring \(\mathbb{Z}/2^{3a}\mathbb{Z}\). These matrices are used to “mask” the torsion point images.

The resulting public system parameter set available to all parties is \(\text{param} = (p, a, b, d_{A,1}, d_1, E_0, \mathcal{O}_0, P_0, Q_0)\).


2.2 Key Generation (Receiver)

Secret Isogeny 1 (\(\phi_{A,1}\)): Using the global parameters, an intermediate curve \(E_{A,1}\) and mapped torsion points \((P_{A,1}, Q_{A,1})\) are generated by executing \(\text{RandIsogImages}_{\mathcal{O}_0}(d_{A,1}, 2^{3a}; P_0, Q_0)\).
Secret Isogeny 2 (\(\phi_{A,2}\)): A random \(3^b\)-isogeny \(\phi_{A,2}\) is computed from \(E_{A,1}\) to the final public curve \(E_A\), mapping the torsion points to \((P_A, Q_A) = (\phi_{A,2}(P_{A,1}), \phi_{A,2}(Q_{A,1}))\).
Masking: A diagonal matrix \(\mathbf{A} \in_U \mathcal{M}_{2^{3a}}\) is chosen uniformly at random. This matrix is used to mask the torsion points, computing \((R_A, S_A)^\top = \mathbf{A}(P_A, Q_A)^\top\).
Keys: The resulting public key is \(\text{pk} = (E_A, R_A, S_A)\), while the secret key is retained as \(\text{sk} = (E_{A,1}, P_{A,1}, Q_{A,1}, \mathbf{A})\).



2.3 Encryption (Sender)

Message Encoding: A message \(m \in \{0, 1\}^{3a-2}\) is treated as an integer \(m \in [0, 2^{3a-2}-1]\). To map this integer bijectively into the invertible elements of the modular ring, the sender maps it to an odd integer: \(s_B = 2m + 1\). The sender then reduces \(s_B \pmod{2^{3a}}\) and calculates its modular inverse \(s_B^{-1} \pmod{2^{3a}}\) to construct the diagonal masking matrix \(\mathbf{B} = \text{diag}(s_B, s_B^{-1}) \in \mathcal{M}_{2^{3a}}\).
Isogeny \(\phi_1\): An isogeny of degree \(d_1\) to curve \(E_1\), alongside mapped points \((P_1, Q_1)\), is generated via \(\text{RandIsogImages}_{\mathcal{O}_0}(d_1, 2^{3a}; P_0, Q_0)\).
First Ciphertext Component: The intermediate points are masked using the encoded matrix \(\mathbf{B}\) to compute \((R_1, S_1)^\top = \mathbf{B}(P_1, Q_1)^\top\).
Isogeny \(\phi_2\): A random \(3^{2b}\)-isogeny \(\phi_2\) is computed from the public key’s curve \(E_A\) to a new curve \(E_2\).
Second Ciphertext Component: The masked points from the public key are evaluated through \(\phi_2\) and further masked by \(\mathbf{B}\) to yield \((R_2, S_2)^\top = \mathbf{B}(\phi_2(R_A), \phi_2(S_A))^\top\).
Output: The final ciphertext encapsulates these elements as \(\text{ct} = (E_1, R_1, S_1, E_2, R_2, S_2)\).



2.4 Decryption (Receiver)

Initialization & Kani’s Criterion: The receiver begins by setting the combined degrees of the parallel isogeny paths: \(N_1 = d_{A,1}d_1\) and \(N_2 = 3^{3b}\). Crucially, the system parameters guarantee that \(N_1 + N_2 = 2^{3a}\), which perfectly matches the \(2^{3a}\)-torsion space and strictly satisfies Kani’s criterion for the subsequent step.
Unmasking Setup: Using the secret matrix \(\mathbf{A}\), the receiver computes the partially unmasked ciphertext points: \((R_2', S_2')^\top = d_1 \mathbf{A}^{-1}(R_2, S_2)^\top\).
Kani’s Evaluation: The core of the decryption uses Kani’s lemma to navigate the commutative isogeny square. To achieve this, the algorithm constructs a higher-dimensional \((2^{3a}, 2^{3a})\)-isogeny originating from the product of the two ciphertext curves, \(E_1 \times E_2\). By combining the points \((R_1, S_1)\) from the first curve and the partially unmasked points \((R_2', S_2')\) from the second curve to form the kernel of this product isogeny, the receiver systematically strips away the outer isogeny layers. This geometric projection recovers the target point images \((R_{A,1}, S_{A,1})\) resting on the intermediate secret curve \(E_{A,1}\).
Matrix Recovery: Kani’s evaluation yields the matrix equation \((R_{A,1}, S_{A,1})^\top = d_1 \mathbf{B}(P_{A,1}, Q_{A,1})^\top\). Because the masking matrix is strictly defined as \(\mathbf{B} = \text{diag}(s_B, s_B^{-1})\), this expands into a direct scalar multiplication: \(R_{A,1} = [d_1 \cdot s_B] P_{A,1}\). The receiver isolates the unknown scalar \(s_B\) by solving this discrete logarithm problem via the \(2^{3a}\)-Tate pairing, which fully reconstructs \(\mathbf{B}\).
Message Decoding: Kani’s evaluation recovers the point images up to a curve automorphism (which is \(\{\pm 1\}\) for standard curves), yielding a modular representative \(s_B\). To resolve the sign ambiguity and step out of the modular ring, the algorithm lifts the value back into a bounded integer: \(s_B = \min(s_B, 2^{3a} - s_B)\). This isolates the exact odd integer \(s_B \in [1, 2^{3a-1}-1]\) chosen during encoding. Finally, using standard integer arithmetic, the original plaintext message is retrieved: \(m = (s_B - 1) / 2\).

3 Security Assumptions
The core OW-CPA security of the QFESTA PKE relies on specialized variants of FESTA’s distinguishing and computational problems.

Pseudorandomness of RandIsogImages: The foundational assumption assumes that the codomain elliptic curve \(E_1\) and its mapped torsion points \((P_1, Q_1)\) produced by RandIsogImages are computationally indistinguishable from a tuple drawn uniformly at random from valid configurations.
Variant DIST Problem: The security proof extends this to the public keys themselves, assuming an adversary cannot distinguish the legitimate masked points \((R_A, S_A)\) on \(E_A\) from uniformly random torsion points.
Hardness of Isogeny Recovery: Finding the secret isogenies (\(\phi_A, \phi_1, \phi_2\)) given the degrees (\(d_A, d_1, d_2\)) requires \(O(2^{\lambda})\) operations classically and \(O(2^{\lambda/2})\) operations via quantum attacks (using Grover’s algorithm or meet-in-the-middle strategies), satisfying the targeted security levels.

title: pSIDH
text:
Broken by a polynomial time quantum algorithm.

The pSIDH (prime-SIDH) scheme is a novel Non-Interactive Key Exchange (NIKE) scheme introduced to circumvent the catastrophic torsion-point attacks that broke smooth-degree isogeny schemes like SIDH and Séta. While SIDH utilizes secret isogenies of smooth degrees to allow for efficient evaluation via Vélu’s formulas, this smooth-degree structure fundamentally enables the polynomial-time attacks. pSIDH transitions the SIDH-style commutative isogeny diagram to the setting of large prime degrees.
Because standard evaluation of large prime-degree isogenies is computationally infeasible, pSIDH relies on a novel cryptographic tool: the suborder representation [Lero22]. In this scheme, secret keys are represented as quaternion ideals (the ideal representation), while public keys are broadcast as suborder representations.

2 Scheme Design
The pSIDH scheme involves two parties, Alice and Bob, agreeing on a shared secret over supersingular elliptic curves.

Here isogenies \([\varphi_A]_* \varphi_B\) and \([\varphi_B]_* \varphi_A\) are defined as the separable isogenies of respective kernels \(\varphi_A(\text{ker}(\varphi_B))\) and \(\varphi_B(\text{ker}(\varphi_A))\).

2.1 Global Parameters

\(p\): A large prime characterizing the field \(\mathbb{F}_{p^2}\).
\(E_0\): A starting supersingular elliptic curve defined over \(\mathbb{F}_{p^2}\).
\(\mathcal{O}_0\): A known maximal order in the quaternion algebra \(B_{p, \infty}\) such that \(\text{End}(E_0) \cong \mathcal{O}_0\).



2.2 Key Generation
Alice selects a large secret prime \(D_A \neq p\).

Secret Key (\(I_A\), \(\varphi_A\)): Alice samples a random integral left-\(\mathcal{O}_0\) ideal \(I_A\) of norm \(D_A\). Through the Deuring correspondence, \(I_A\) represents a cyclic isogeny \(\varphi_A: E_0 \to E_A\) of degree \(D_A\).
Public Key (\(E_A, \pi_A\)): Alice computes the suborder representation \(\pi_A = \text{IdealToSuborder}(I_A)\). This representation consists of the codomain curve \(E_A\) and a collection of endomorphisms that reveal a specific suborder \(\mathbb{Z} + D_A \mathcal{O}_0\) embedded within \(\text{End}(E_A)\).

Bob symmetrically generates his keys using a distinct prime \(D_B\), producing an ideal \(I_B\) (corresponding to \(\varphi_B: E_0 \to E_B\)) and public key \((E_B, \pi_B)\).


2.3 Key Exchange
To compute the shared curve \(E\), Alice uses Bob’s public key \((E_B, \pi_B)\) alongside her secret key \(I_A\). Because Alice cannot directly compute the push-forward isogeny \([\varphi_B]_* \varphi_A : E_B \to E_{AB}\) due to \(D_A\) being a large prime, she relies on an auxiliary smooth-degree path to reach \(E\):

Alice uses the algorithm IdealSuborderNormEquation to find an element \(\theta \in (\mathbb{Z} + D_B \mathcal{O}_0) \cap I_A\) with norm \(D_A \cdot S\), where \(S\) is a carefully chosen powersmooth integer. Moreover, because \(\theta \in I_A\), under the Deuring correspondence it maps to an endomorphism on \(E_0\) that factors through her secret isogeny \(\varphi_A\). That is, the endomorphism \(\theta\) can be written as \(\sigma_A \circ \varphi_A\), where \(\sigma_A : E_A \to E_0\) is an auxiliary isogeny of smooth degree \(S\).
By pushing this endomorphism forward through Bob’s isogeny \(\varphi_B\), Alice utilizes Bob’s suborder representation \(\pi_B\) to obtain an embedding \(\iota_B(\theta)\) into \(\text{End}(E_B)\).
This embedded endomorphism on \(E_B\) is equivalent to \(\psi_A \circ [\varphi_B]_*\varphi_A\), where \(\psi_A: E_{AB} \to E_B\) is an auxiliary isogeny of degree \(S\).
Since \(S\) is smooth, Alice can use the SuborderEvaluation algorithm on this endomorphism to explicitly find the kernel of the dual isogeny \(\hat{\psi}_A : E_B \to E_{AB}\).
Taking the quotient by this kernel, Alice computes the isogeny \(\hat{\psi}_A\). The codomain of \(\hat{\psi}_A\) is the target shared curve \(E_{AB}\), satisfying the commutativity of the diagram.
Symmetrically, Bob computes an analogous auxiliary isogeny \(\hat{\psi}_B: E_A \to E_{AB}\) using Alice’s public key and his secret key.

Both parties arrive at the identical curve \(E_{AB}\), allowing them to use the \(j\)-invariant \(j(E_{AB})\) as the shared secret.

title: pSIDH
text:
3 Security Assumptions
The core security of pSIDH is tied to the SubOrder to Ideal Problem (SOIP), which relates more closely to the key recovery of CSIDH (involving partial endomorphism ring knowledge) than that of SIDH, yet maintains an SIDH-like key agreement flow.

SubOrder to Ideal Problem (SOIP): This is the underlying key recovery assumption. It states that given a suborder representation \(\pi\) of an isogeny \(\varphi\) of prime degree \(D\), it is computationally infeasible to recover the ideal representation \(I_\varphi\) (the secret key). Because the degree \(D\) is a large prime, the \(D\)-torsion points are defined over an exponentially large field extension \(\mathbb{F}_{p^k}\) (where \(k = O(D)\)). This prevents the polynomial-time torsion point attacks that devastated SIDH from being applied to SOIP. However, there is a sub-exponential quantum attack against the SOIP.
prime Supersingular Decisional Diffie-Hellman (pSSDDH): The semantic security of the key exchange relies on this decisional assumption. pSSDDH assumes that an adversary cannot distinguish the valid shared curve \(E_{AB}\) (where \(\text{End}(E_{AB}) \cong \mathcal{O}_R(I_A \cap I_B)\)) from a random curve \(E_C\) that is merely \(D_A D_B\)-isogenous to \(E_0\). This assumption directly borrows its structural formulation from the SSDDH problem introduced in the original SIDH proposal, but strictly limits the isogeny degrees to large primes and leverages suborder representations rather than torsion point images.

title: POKÉ
text: POKÉ is a public-key encryption scheme constructed from isogenies of unknown degrees. The primary motivation behind POKÉ is to bridge two distinct paradigms in isogeny-based cryptography: the traditional one-dimensional SIDH-like commutative diagrams, and the newer, higher-dimensional representations (such as those used in FESTA or SQIsignHD) [BaMa25]. By having one party compute isogenies of an unknown, non-smooth degree (requiring higher-dimensional representation techniques to evaluate) and the other party compute smooth-degree isogenies (with kernel generators defined over the base field), POKÉ establishes a commutative diagram where all four elliptic curves are made public. Despite the curves being known, the scheme achieves a shared secret by exploiting the commutativity of the hidden isogenies evaluated on a set of auxiliary torsion points. This structural choice completely circumvents the polynomial-time attacks that broke SIDH, which intrinsically require the exact degree of the targeted isogeny to be known.

The scheme is built on a finite field where the parameters scale strictly with the targeted security parameter \(\lambda\).

\(p\): A prime characteristic \(p = 2^a 3^b 5^c f - 1\).

\(a \approx \lambda\): Bounds the search space for the Alice’s secret degree \(q(2^a - q)\). \(a \approx \lambda\) ensures brute-forcing the unknown degree is exponentially hard.
\(3^b \approx 2^{2\lambda}\): The known degree of the Bob’s isogeny. It is sized to prevent meet-in-the-middle key-recovery attacks while keeping evaluations fast.
\(5^c \approx 2^{\lambda/3}\): The order of the shared secret points. It provides exactly enough entropy to prevent an attacker from guessing the three unknown change-of-basis coefficients.

\(E_0\): A supersingular elliptic curve over \(\mathbb{F}_{p^2}\) with \(j\)-invariant 1728.
Bases: \((P_0, Q_0) \in E_0[2^a]\), \((R_0, S_0) \in E_0[3^b]\), and \((X_0, Y_0) \in E_0[5^c]\).
\(\text{KDF}\): A standard key derivation function.



2.2 Key Generation (Alice)

Secret Variables:

\(q \in [1, 2^a - 1]\): A random integer coprime to 2, 3, and 5.
\(\phi: E_0 \to E_A\): The secret isogeny of degree \(q(2^a - q)\) is generated by adapting RandIsogImages algorithm proposed in QFESTA.
\(\alpha_2, \beta_2 \in (\mathbb{Z}/2^a\mathbb{Z})^\times\): Independent diagonal masking scalars.
\(\gamma_3 \in (\mathbb{Z}/3^b\mathbb{Z})^\times, \delta_5 \in (\mathbb{Z}/5^c\mathbb{Z})^\times\): Uniform masking scalars.

Masked Points on \(E_A\):

\(2^a\)-torsion: \(P_A = [\alpha_2]\phi(P_0), \quad Q_A = [\beta_2]\phi(Q_0)\)
\(3^b\)-torsion: \(R_A = [\gamma_3]\phi(R_0), \quad S_A = [\gamma_3]\phi(S_0)\)
\(5^c\)-torsion: \(X_A = [\delta_5]\phi(X_0), \quad Y_A = [\delta_5]\phi(Y_0)\)

Output:

Public Key: \((E_A, P_A, Q_A, R_A, S_A, X_A, Y_A)\)
Secret Key: \((q, \alpha_2, \beta_2, \delta_5)\) alongside the higher-dimensional representation of \(\phi\).




2.3 Encryption (Bob)

Secret Variables:

\(r_3 \in \mathbb{Z}/3^b\mathbb{Z}\): An ephemeral scalar to define the isogeny kernel.
\(\omega_2 \in (\mathbb{Z}/2^a\mathbb{Z})^\times\): A masking scalar to prevent pairing leakage.
\(\mathbf{D}_5 \in SL_2(\mathbb{Z}/5^c\mathbb{Z})\): A determinant-1 masking matrix.

Parallel Isogenies:

\(\psi: E_0 \to E_B\): Degree \(3^b\) isogeny with kernel \(\langle R_0 + [r_3]S_0 \rangle\).
\(\psi': E_A \to E_{AB}\): Pushforward isogeny \([\phi]_*\psi\) with kernel \(\langle R_A + [r_3]S_A \rangle=\phi(\mathrm{ker}(\psi))\).

Masked Points on \(E_B\) and \(E_{AB}\):

\(P_B = [\omega_2]\psi(P_0), \quad Q_B = [1/\omega_2]\psi(Q_0)\)
\(P_{AB} = [\omega_2]\psi'(P_A), \quad Q_{AB} = [1/\omega_2]\psi'(Q_A)\)
\([X_B, Y_B]^T = \mathbf{D}_5[\psi(X_0), \psi(Y_0)]^T\)

Shared Secret Points:

\([X_{AB}, Y_{AB}]^T = \mathbf{D}_5[\psi'(X_A), \psi'(Y_A)]^T\)

Message Encoding:

\(ct' = m \oplus \text{KDF}(X_{AB}, Y_{AB})\)

Output:

Ciphertext: \(((E_B, P_B, Q_B, X_B, Y_B), (E_{AB}, P_{AB}, Q_{AB}), ct')\)




2.4 Decryption (Alice)
The goal of decryption is for Alice (receiver) to push the Bob’s (sender) points \((X_B, Y_B)\) through their secret pushforward isogeny \(\phi': E_B \to E_{AB}\) to reconstruct the shared secret \((X_{AB}, Y_{AB})\).

Unmask Anchor Points:

Compute \(P'_{AB} = [1/\alpha_2]P_{AB}\) and \(Q'_{AB} = [1/\beta_2]Q_{AB}\).

Construct 2D Isogeny (\(\Phi'\)):

Define kernel \(\langle([-q]P_B, P'_{AB}), ([-q]Q_B, Q'_{AB})\rangle\).
Apply Kani’s Theorem to generate a 2-dimensional isogeny matrix \(\Phi': E_B \times E_{AB} \to F \times F'\).

2D Evaluation:

Embed input points as \((X_B, \mathcal{O}_{E_{AB}})\) and \((Y_B, \mathcal{O}_{E_{AB}})\).
Evaluate via \(\Phi'\) to obtain points \(X'_B\) and \(Y'_B\) on the intermediate curve \(F\).

Coordinate Translation:

Generate a reference basis \((U, V)\) on \(E_{AB}\).
Embed and evaluate \((\mathcal{O}_{E_B}, U)\) and \((\mathcal{O}_{E_B}, V)\) via \(\Phi'\) to obtain basis \(U'\) and \(V'\) on \(F\).
Solve discrete logarithms in \(\mathbb{Z}_{5^c}\) to find coefficients \(x, y, w, z\) such that:

\(X'_B = [x]U' + [y]V'\)
\(Y'_B = [w]U' + [z]V'\)


Reconstruct Shared Secret: Compute target points on \(E_{AB}\):

\(X_{AB} = [\delta_5][2^a-q]([x]U + [y]V)\)
\(Y_{AB} = [\delta_5][2^a-q]([w]U + [z]V)\)

Message Decoding: \(m = ct' \oplus \text{KDF}(X_{AB}, Y_{AB})\)

text:
3 Security Assumptions

C-POKE Problem (Computational): Given the public transcripts of Key Generation and Encryption, an adversary cannot efficiently compute the shared secret points \(X_{AB}\) and \(Y_{AB}\). It relies on the hardness of recovering either secret isogeny.
D-POKE Problem (Decisional): An adversary cannot distinguish the true shared secret points \((X_{AB}, Y_{AB})\) from a pair of random points on \(E_{AB}[5^c]\) with identical Weil pairings. (Required for standard-model IND-CPA security).
Receiver’s Isogeny Security: The use of an unknown degree \(q(2^a-q)\) combined with independent diagonal masking (\(\alpha_2 \neq \beta_2\)) breaks the structural prerequisites needed for known pairing-based or torsion-exploiting attacks.
Sender’s Isogeny Security: The hardness of recovering the sender’s isogeny \(\psi\) from diagonally scaled target points reduces to a parallel variant of the CIST problem.
Heuristic Key Generation Indistinguishability: If the optimized heuristic approach is used for Key Generation, it relies on the assumption that the output curve is computationally indistinguishable from a uniformly sampled \(q(2^a-q)\)-isogenous curve.

title: TOGA-UE
text: The development of Updatable Encryption (UE) schemes using post-quantum group actions has historically been bottlenecked by the requirement for Mappable Effective Group Actions (MEGA). In the isogeny setting, instantiating a MEGA is practically infeasible due to the notorious difficulty of hashing into the set of supersingular elliptic curves. The TOGA-UE (Triple Orbital Group Action Updatable Encryption) scheme circumvents this limitation by drawing inspiration from the SiGamal encryption scheme [LeRo24]. Instead of attempting to map messages directly to an isogeny graph vertex (a curve), TOGA-UE maps messages as scalars to specific points on an elliptic curve via scalar multiplication. The underlying curve and the points are then transformed using the isogeny group action. This architectural shift eliminates the need to hash into supersingular curves while natively supporting an unbounded number of ciphertext updates. Consequently, TOGA-UE instantiated from CSIDH stands as the first post-quantum UE scheme that is not based on lattices and places no limits on key rotations.

title: TOGA-UE
text:
2 Scheme Design
TOGA-UE is built upon an abstract algebraic framework known as an Effective Triple Orbital Group Action (ETOGA). To instantiate this from CSIDH, the scheme defines specific group actions operating over supersingular curves enriched with torsion point information.

2.1 System Setup
This algorithm takes the security parameter \(\lambda\) as input (which dictates the sizes of the underlying cryptographic structures) and establishes the public parameters and mathematical framework for the CSIDH instantiation.

Define the Field and Curve: Based on \(\lambda\), choose a large prime \(p \equiv 3 \pmod 4\) and define the base supersingular elliptic curve \(E_0: y^2 = x^3 + x\) over \(\mathbb{F}_p\).
Establish the Order and Torsion: Let \(\mathfrak{O} = \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-p}]\) be the quadratic order corresponding to the Frobenius endomorphism ring. Choose a smooth integer \(N\) (sized according to \(\lambda\)), split in \(\mathfrak{O}\) and coprime to the ideal factor base.
Define the State Space (\(S\)): Let \(S\) be the set of elements \((E, \iota, P)\), where \(E\) is a supersingular curve, \(\iota\) is an \(\mathfrak{O}\)-orientation, and \(P \in E[N]\) is a point of order \(N\). Fix a public origin state \(s_0 \in S\) using \(E_0\), its canonical orientation, and a deterministic base point \(P_0 \in E_0[N]\).
Define the Main Group Action (\(*_A\)) and Sample Space (\(A'\)): Let \(A\) be a subgroup of fractional \(\mathfrak{O}\)-ideals generated by small prime ideals \(\mathfrak{l}_1, \dots, \mathfrak{l}_n\). Define a finite subset \(A' \subset A\) bounded by a small exponent maximum \(m\) (i.e., ideals with exponents \(\in [-m, m]\)) to allow efficient, near-uniform sampling. For an ideal \(\mathfrak{a} \in A\), define its action as evaluating an isogeny: \(\mathfrak{a} *_A (E, \iota, P) = (E_{\mathfrak{a}}, \iota_{\mathfrak{a}}, \varphi_{\mathfrak{a}}^E(P))\).
Define the Orbital Group Action (\(*_H\)): Let \(H = (\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^\times\). Define the action of \(h \in H\) as scalar multiplication on the order-\(N\) point: \(h *_H (E, \iota, P) = (E, \iota, [h]P)\).
Establish Helper Functions:

Define \(\sim_A\) as the congruence relation where ideals are equivalent if they share the same ideal class.
Define \(\text{Reduce}_A\) to output a short, canonical representative of an ideal’s equivalence class.
Define \(\text{Reduce}_S\) to output a canonical representative for an equivalence class in \(S\) under the orbital action.
Define \(\text{Invert}_H\) as an efficient algorithm that computes the discrete logarithm between two points in \(E[N]\) to invert the group action \(*_H\).
Define \(\psi\) as an efficiently invertible map from the message space \(\mathcal{M}\) to \(H\).
Define \(h(\cdot, \cdot)\) as a function computing a structural modifier in \(H\) to correct discrepancies during ideal reduction.

Output: The public parameters \(pp = (A, A', H, S, s_0, *_A, \sim_A, *_H, \psi, \text{Reduce}_A, \text{Reduce}_S, \text{Invert}_H)\).



2.2 Key Generation
Generates an epoch encryption key \(k_e\) using the public parameters \(pp\).

Sample a bounded ideal vector \(a' \leftarrow A'\) and a scalar \(h \leftarrow H\).
Return \(k_e = (\text{Reduce}_A(a'), h) \in A \times H\).



2.3 Encryption
Encrypts a message \(M \in \mathcal{M}\) under epoch key \(k_e = (a_e, h_e)\).

Sample a random, bounded ideal \(r' \leftarrow A'\).
Compute reduced ideal \(r = \text{Reduce}_A(r')\).
Calculate the base state \(s = \text{Reduce}_S(r *_A s_0)\).
Return ciphertext \(C_e = (\psi(M)h_e) *_H (a_e *_A s)\).



2.4 Token Generation
Generates the update token \(\Delta_{e+1}\) used to transition ciphertexts from epoch \(e\) to \(e+1\) given keys \(k_e\) and \(k_{e+1}\).

Parse \(k_e = (a_e, h_e)\) and \(k_{e+1} = (a_{e+1}, h_{e+1})\).
Compute the ideal transition \(c_e = \text{Reduce}_A(a_e^{-1}a_{e+1})\).
Compute the structural modifier \(h' = h(a_e^{-1}a_{e+1}, c_e^{-1})\).
Return update token \(\Delta_{e+1} = (c_e, h' h_{e+1} h_e^{-1})\).



2.5 Ciphertext Update
Deterministically updates a ciphertext \(C_e\) from epoch \(e\) to \(e+1\) using the server-side token \(\Delta_{e+1}\).

Parse \(\Delta_{e+1} = (a, h)\).
Return updated ciphertext \(C_{e+1} = h *_H (a *_A C_e)\).



2.6 Decryption
Decrypts ciphertext \(C_e\) using epoch key \(k_e = (a_e, h_e)\).

Compute the inverse ideal \(b_e = \text{Reduce}_A(a_e^{-1})\) and modifier \(h' = h(a_e, b_e)\).
Undo the key’s actions: \(s' = (h_e h')^{-1} *_H (b_e *_A C_e)\).
Recover the canonical representative \(s = \text{Reduce}_S(s')\).
Extract the message by solving the discrete logarithm in the smooth-order group \(E[N]\): \(M' = \psi^{-1}(\text{Invert}_H(s', s))\).
Return \(M'\).

title: TOGA-UE
text:
3 Security Assumptions
The detIND-UE-CPA (Deterministic Updates Indistinguishability - Updatable Encryption - Chosen Plaintext Attack) confidentiality of the TOGA-UE scheme directly relies on specific computational hardness properties embedded within the group action. Notably, TOGA-UE is a promising approach because it avoids reliance on the ideal cipher model. However, its security relies on the weak pseudorandomness of the entire TOGA structure. The core security assumptions and their nuances are detailed below:

Extended Weak Pseudorandomness (P-CSSDDH Connection): The core problem assumed to be computationally hard is distinguishing tuples of the form \((s_i, \mathfrak{a} *_A s_i)\) from tuples of the form \((s_i, t_i)\), where \(\mathfrak{a} \leftarrow \mathcal{D}_A\) is a secret ideal and \(s_i, t_i \leftarrow \mathcal{D}_S\) are random elements from the state space \(S\). This instantiation based on CSIDH closely aligns with the P-CSSDDH assumption.
Irreducibility to Standard CSIDH: Standard isogeny-based group actions assume the weak pseudorandomness of the induced class group action (\(*_G\)) operating purely on oriented curves. Unfortunately, the P-CSSDDH assumption does not reduce to the standard weak pseudorandomness of CSIDH because additional torsion point information is revealed in the extended state space \(S\).
Resilience and Uncertainty: The revealed torsion point information makes the exact hardness of P-CSSDDH less well understood compared to standard CSIDH. However, this revealed information is not sufficient to apply the catastrophic torsion-point attacks that broke SIDH. The degree of the secret isogeny remains unknown and uniform over a large sample, which invalidates standard Weil pairing or genus-theory reduction attacks.

title: LIT-SiGamal
text: LIT-SiGamal is a public key encryption (PKE) scheme that constructs an ElGamal-like mechanism over supersingular elliptic curve isogenies by combining the structural approach of SiGamal with the Long Isogeny with Torsion (LIT) diagram framework [MoSt25]. The original SiGamal scheme relied on a commutative CSIDH-based diagram to enable the sender and receiver to compute parallel isogenies without revealing their secret paths. However, CSIDH-based constructions require computing group actions over extremely large primes (often exceeding 3,000 bits for baseline security), rendering them highly inefficient. LIT-SiGamal bypasses this bottleneck by replacing the CSIDH diagram with a LIT diagram, a commutative diagram parameterized to consist of large-degree horizontal isogenies and relatively low-degree vertical isogenies. To make the bottom isogeny computable without knowledge of the vertical secret isogenies, LIT-SiGamal incorporates auxiliary torsion points masked by matrices, a technique adapted from the FESTA scheme. This design allows for significantly smaller primes and faster execution times while maintaining robust post-quantum security. Moreover, the constructions of POKÉ and LIT-SiGamal are nearly identical, with the key distinction being the degree of the isogeny used in the public key: POKÉ employs an isogeny of degree approximately \(2^{2\lambda}\), whereas LIT-SiGamal uses one of degree approximately \(2^{6\lambda}\).

text:
2 Scheme Design
The LIT-SiGamal protocol operates over a carefully structured prime field and relies on the exchange of evaluated torsion bases to enable a shared commutative diagram.
